# Terms and Conditions

1. All participants should register for this benchmark with their real names, affiliations (including department, full name of university/institute/company, country), and affiliation E-mails. Incomplete and redundant registrations will be removed without notice. Each team can have at most six people.

2. All participant must provide a GitHub repository. If your method isn't possible to replicate using the repository it will be removed. 

3. All participants agree to make the results of the benchmark public.

4. The dataset is shared under the Creative Common Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International License. You can read the full license in the LICENSE.md when downloading the dataset.

If the competition manager suspect cheating, the participant will be removed from the competition.

pages.title: Participation
pages.content:
## SingleTree Project The SingleTree project aims to create a smarter forestry system by focusing on individual trees. This approach will help forests adapt to climate change, become more resilient, and allow for more sustainable use of wood resources. SingleTree will develop advanced methods to monitor forests based on artificial intelligence and remote sensing, adaptive single-tree level management solutions, intelligent machines for implementing single-tree operations, and improved traceability and ability to predict wood quality early in the value chain as a foundation for optimised biomass supply. To read more, visit https://singletree.eu/
## Update 2026-11-09 Participants reported errors in the reference labels, and we have updated the competition in accordance. Thank you for the report! * **New dataset version:** FOR-wood v2 is on Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24083541) with corrected whorl and stem labels. The trees, the train/test split and the point clouds are unchanged, so you only need the new training labels. Re-train if you used the v1 labels. * **New scoring rules:** whorl detection is now ranked by **Skill**, and both tasks have stricter rules for missing trees and heights. See [Evaluation](#evaluation) below. * **Leaderboard rescored:** all existing submissions have been rerun on the corrected test labels with the new scorer, so scores and ranks may have changed. You don't need to resubmit. * **Co-authorship:** the top 2 by whorl Skill and the top 2 by stem RMSE are invited and one more team is invited depending on the task with the most unique team submissions, ranked separately. See [Prize](#prize). * **More submissions:** because of this update, we decided to increase the number of submissions per day to **4** and the total number of submissions to **50**. # Objective of the benchmark The objective of this benchmark is to gather and evaluate the performance of sensor- and platform-agnostic whorl detection and stem profile algorithms. The result will provide the SingleTree project with methods that can be used further down the project chain. # Prize Five teams will have the opportunity to co-author an article about this benchmark. Each team can nominate up to two people as co-authors. The places are given per task: * the **top 2** teams by **Skill** (whorl detection), and * the **top 2** teams by **RMSE (Stem)** (stem profile estimation). * one more team from the task that gets the most unique team submissions The two tasks are ranked separately, so you can compete in one or both. A team that places in both counts once, and the next team on the stem ranking moves up. Ranks are taken from the leaderboard at the end of the Benchmark Phase, among submissions that follow the terms. Teams in co-authorship positions will be contacted at the start of the Review Phase and asked to provide a GitHub repository for their method (see Terms). # How to participate ## Read the terms for entering Go to the terms tab under Get Started and read the terms for entering. If you fail to follow these terms, you will be removed from the competition. In your submission, you MUST provide name, affiliation (with contact information) and a short description of the method with a link to a GitHub repository. ## Download the dataset The dataset, **FOR-wood**, is available for download from Zenodo: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24083541 The dataset were updated on 2026-11-09 to version 2.0 ## Benchmarking For evaluation the participant should use their model on the downloaded test set to predict either whorl-positions relative to the ground, the stem profile diameter, or both and output two tables (*.csv) containing predictions for all trees in the test data set. For the whorl detection task, submit a `branch_references.csv` table with the following columns and capitalization: `TreeID`, `Z`, `whorl_number` The scorer matches predictions using `TreeID` and `Z`, where `Z` is the whorl height in metres and `whorl_number` identifies the whorl order. |TreeID|Z|whorl_number| |---|---|---| |221|10.8434|1| |221|11.2577|2| |221|11.5477|3| |n|...|...| For the stem profile prediction task, submit a `stem_references.csv` table with the following columns and capitalization: `TreeID`, `Z`, `D` `Z` is the height in metres and `D` is the predicted stem diameter in metres. Provide values at 0.6 m, 1.3 m, 2 m, and then every metre up the length of the tree. If values are not provided exactly at the evaluation heights, the scorer linearly interpolates the submitted profile. |TreeID|Z|D| |---|---|---| |313|0.4903|0.30539| |313|1.1375|0.29004| |313|1.8426|0.27856| |313|4.8407|0.25084| |n|...|...| Make sure that the column names are exactly the same as stated here. The zip archive itself can be named anything, but it may contain either or both CSV files, and each included file must use its exact corresponding filename: ```text your_submission.zip ├── branch_references.csv └── stem_references.csv ``` # Evaluation Every tree in the test set is scored, in both tasks. A tree that is missing from your submission counts as a complete miss, so submit predictions for all test trees. ## Whorl detection For each tree, your predicted whorl heights (`Z`) are matched one-to-one with the reference whorls. A prediction counts as correct (a true positive) if it lies within **±5 cm** of a reference whorl; the matching finds the largest possible number of such pairs. From this, each tree gets a precision, recall and F1 score. When several pairings are possible, the scorer first finds the largest number of pairs within ±5 cm, and among those the one with the smallest total height error, so adding or removing one prediction cannot shift the other pairs. * **Above the tree's top label:** predictions more than 5 cm above a tree's highest reference whorl are ignored, because the trees are only labelled up to that height. * **Below:** there is no lower limit, so predictions below the lowest reference whorl count as false positives. The leaderboard ranks whorl detection by **Skill**, the improvement over a blind baseline: Skill = (F1 − F1comb) / (1 − F1comb) * **The comb** is a guess that ignores the point cloud: whorls evenly spaced from a fixed start height to the top of the tree, with the spacing and start height tuned per source on the training data. * **What Skill means:** a comb scores **0**, a perfect submission scores **1**, and a submission worse than the comb is negative. It shows how much better than guessing a method is, independent of how easy a source is to guess. * **Per source:** Skill is computed for each data source (**FI**, **NO**, **SE**) from the mean F1 over that source's trees. The leaderboard's **Skill** is the mean of the three, so each source counts equally however many trees it has. You can tell the source from the tree ID: numbers only = FI, `plot…` = NO, all others = SE. **Precision**, **Recall** and **MAE** (mean absolute height error of the matched whorls, in meters) are shown for information. They are averages over all test trees. ## Stem profile Diameters are compared at **0.6 m, 1.3 m, 2 m, 3 m, …**, every meter, within the height range of each tree's reference profile. Your profile is linearly interpolated to these heights, but it is **not extended** beyond your lowest and highest submitted values: at an evaluation height your profile doesn't cover, your diameter counts as **0**, so the error is the full reference diameter. Submit profiles from the ground up to the top of the stem. * **RMSE (Stem)** is the root mean square diameter error (m) over all evaluation heights of all trees. It ranks the stem task. * **Bias (Stem)** is the mean of predicted minus reference diameter (m). A positive value means too thick. It is shown for information, and 0 is ideal. ## Submission limits You may submit up to 4 times per day (50 total for the phase). This limit is increased in the new update. from the original 2 per day and 20 total. ## Viewing your results After submitting, publish your result to the leaderboard from your submissions panel. The leaderboard is sorted by Skill (whorl detection) by default - if you only submitted stem profile predictions, click on a stem profile column header (e.g. RMSE (Stem)) to sort the leaderboard by that metric instead and see where your submission ranks.

pages.title: Dataset
pages.content:
# Dataset
For this benchmark, we have assembled a dataset consisting of indivdual tree point clouds together with annotations describing whorl positions along the stem as well as stem taper. The data has been pooled from Sweden, Finland and Norway and consists mainly of Scott's Pine trees with a smaller proportion Norway Spruce. 

The dataset, **FOR-wood**, is available for download from Zenodo: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24083541

The data consist of:
* **Training data**: tree point clouds (laz files) with whorl and taper annotations (`branch_references.csv`, `stem_references.csv`)
* **Test data**: only tree point clouds (laz files), no annotations

**License:** [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/) (Attribution-ShareAlike). You may share and adapt the dataset, even commercially, as long as you give appropriate credit and license any derivative datasets under the same terms.
